Taking rivals besides God is followed by seeing that all power belongs to God and that punishment is severe.

Leaving darkness for light broadly opposes the wrongdoers' condition but adds no judgment detail.

Successive communities enter the Fire together and are told that each has a doubled punishment, a close parallel to shared penal consequence.
At the universal appearance before God, followers and leaders exchange blame while the leaders deny any power to help them.
Satan disowns the people who followed him and states that neither side can aid the other, directly explaining why their shared fate offers no benefit.
The weak and arrogant argue together in the Fire, making the focus's shared punishment concrete as mutual blame without relief.
Those in the Fire acknowledge that all are in it together and that the judgment has already been decided.
The invoked partners neither answer nor possess the call, and on the Day of Resurrection they deny the association itself.
Those destroyed had wronged themselves, and their alleged gods did not benefit them when God's command came.
On the trumpet day, family ties no longer avail and people cannot ask after one another, closely framing the loss of relational benefit.
On the gathering day, those worshipped are confronted with the people who worshipped them, exposing the failed association behind judgment.
The question about the objects they used to worship exposes their absence at the moment of final reckoning.
The condemned turn on one another in questioning, supplying the immediate mutual-blame setting that culminates in shared punishment.
The deceivers admit having led the others astray, sharpening the shared responsibility stated in the following ayah.
Followers see the punishment, their ties are severed, and they wish for a return to disown those they followed.
Those called as alleged partners do not answer, and a destructive barrier is placed between them and their claims.
The beings treated as gods will deny their worship and become opponents, showing the reversal of false allegiance.
Wrongdoers are stopped before their Lord and return blame to one another, closely anticipating the helpless shared judgment scene.
The arrogant deny coercion and assign responsibility back to the weak, clarifying why mutual blame does not remove guilt.
The parties will dispute before their Lord on the Day of Resurrection, providing the wider setting of accountability.
Hell lies ahead of those who mocked God's signs, and neither their gains nor their taken protectors avail them.
The inhabitants of the Blaze admit that hearing or reason would have kept them from their final condition.
No intercession of intercessors benefits the condemned, directly reinforcing the focus's denial of benefit at judgment.
